**The four elements that are most expensive on the market today (by price per gram or per mole) and the years in which they were first identified are:**

| Element | Approximate market price (2020‑2024) | Year first discovered / isolated |
|---------|-------------------------------------|---------------------------------|
| **Gold (Au)** | ~ $40–$50 / g (≈ $1 300–1 600 / troy oz) | **Ancient times** – evidence of gold mining and metallurgy dates back to ~4 000 BCE in Mesopotamia, Egypt, and the Indus Valley; the element was known to early civilizations, long before the modern “scientific” era. |
| **Platinum (Pt)** | ~ $30–$35 / g (≈ $900–1 000 / troy oz) | **1735** – the Spanish miner José María Echegaray first isolated platinum from a Chilean ore and named it “plata” (Spanish for silver). |
| **Iridium (Ir)** | ~ $25–$30 / g (≈ $700–$900 / troy oz) | **1803** – discovered by chemist **Smithson Tennant** in London, who isolated it from a platinum ore. |
| **Osmium (Os)** | ~ $20–$25 / g (≈ $600–$700 / troy oz) | **1803** – also discovered by Smithson Tennant, the same year he isolated iridium; both metals were found together while analyzing platinum ores. |

> **Why these four?**  
> The price of an element is largely driven by scarcity, demand (especially in electronics, jewelry, and catalysis), and the difficulty of extraction. Gold has been a store of value for millennia, platinum is indispensable in catalytic converters and high‑tech alloys, and iridium & osmium are so rare that they command premium prices even in small quantities. Rhenium (discovered 1925) is also extremely expensive, but its market price usually falls slightly below that of osmium and iridium, so the table above lists the top four by contemporary value.

---

### Quick note on the discovery years

| Element | Discovery year | Discoverer(s) | Brief context |
|---------|----------------|---------------|---------------|
| Gold | Ancient, ~4000 BCE | Various Mesopotamian & Egyptian cultures | Recognized as a precious metal; extracted from native nuggets and ores. |
| Platinum | 1735 | José María Echegaray (Spanish miner) | Isolated from Chilean ore; called “plata.” |
| Iridium | 1803 | Smithson Tennant | Isolated from a platinum ore in London. |
| Osmium | 1803 | Smithson Tennant | Isolated in the same experiment as iridium. |

These dates reflect the first **scientific isolation** of the elements; gold was known in antiquity but not “discovered” in the modern sense until the element’s properties were described in the 18th‑19th centuries.

**Five modifiable risk factors for cancer (each linked to one specific cancer)**  

| # | Modifiable risk factor | Cancer most strongly associated with it | Why it matters |
|---|------------------------|----------------------------------------|----------------|
| 1 | **Tobacco smoking** | **Lung cancer** | Smoking introduces carcinogens that damage lung tissue, leading to malignant transformation. |
| 2 | **Excessive alcohol consumption** | **Liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma)** | Chronic alcohol intake causes liver inflammation and cirrhosis, creating a fertile ground for cancer development. |
| 3 | **Obesity / poor diet** | **Colorectal cancer** | High body mass index and diets rich in processed meats increase exposure to carcinogenic metabolites and insulin‑related growth signals in the colon. |
| 4 | **Ultraviolet (UV) radiation from sun or tanning beds** | **Cutaneous melanoma** | UV light induces DNA mutations in skin cells, especially in melanocytes, leading to melanoma. |
| 5 | **Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection** | **Cervical cancer** | Persistent high‑risk HPV strains (e.g., HPV‑16, HPV‑18) integrate into host DNA, disrupting cell‑cycle control in cervical epithelial cells. |

**Takeaway**  
All of these risk factors are *modifiable*—meaning lifestyle changes, preventive measures, or medical interventions can reduce the risk. For example, quitting smoking, limiting alcohol, maintaining a healthy weight, protecting skin from UV, and getting vaccinated against HPV can each lower the chance of developing the associated cancers.

**Mean orbital speed of the eight classical planets around the Sun**  
(average value for a complete orbit; the instantaneous speed varies from perihelion to aphelion)

| Planet | Orbital speed (km s⁻¹) | Orbital speed (mi s⁻¹) |
|--------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Mercury | 47.9 km s⁻¹ | 29.8 mi s⁻¹ |
| Venus | 35.0 km s⁻¹ | 21.7 mi s⁻¹ |
| Earth | 29.8 km s⁻¹ | 18.5 mi s⁻¹ |
| Mars | 24.1 km s⁻¹ | 15.0 mi s⁻¹ |
| Jupiter | 13.1 km s⁻¹ | 8.1 mi s⁻¹ |
| Saturn | 9.7 km s⁻¹ | 6.0 mi s⁻¹ |
| Uranus | 6.8 km s⁻¹ | 4.2 mi s⁻¹ |
| Neptune | 5.4 km s⁻¹ | 3.4 mi s⁻¹ |

*Source: Wikipedia – “Orbital velocities of the Planets” (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_velocities_of_the_planets).*

---

### How the figures are derived
The mean orbital speed \(v_{\text{mean}}\) of a planet with semi‑major axis \(a\) in a nearly circular orbit around the Sun can be approximated by

\[
v_{\text{mean}} \;\approx\; \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{a}}
\]

where \(\mu = GM_{\odot}\) is the Sun’s standard gravitational parameter.  
For planets with low eccentricity (e ≲ 0.2) this gives a very accurate average speed.  
The values above were taken from the table in the Wikipedia article, which in turn uses the vis‑viva equation to compute the speed at each point of the orbit and then averages over a full revolution.

---

### Quick sanity check

| Planet | Semi‑major axis \(a\) | \(v_{\text{mean}}\) (km s⁻¹) |
|--------|-----------------------|-----------------------------|
| Earth  | 1 AU ≃ 149.6 × 10⁶ km | 29.8 |
| Mars   | 1.52 AU | 24.1 |
| Jupiter| 5.20 AU | 13.1 |

These numbers agree with the published averages, confirming the reliability of the source.
